title: denali: the no-biology floor for gene-set rankings
description:
denali measures how much of a gene-set ranking is explained by how the sets were constructed — chiefly their size — rather than by biology.

It ships four things a stranger can run: an audit reporting that share with a verdict and a percentile against 1,272 published human CRISPR screens; a re-ranking that applies the size correction and shows which entries the original ranking cannot justify; a baseline that scores a size-only predictor on the caller's own evaluation metric, so that “our model beats baseline” becomes a number someone else can reproduce; and an atlas of per-screen no-biology floors, looked up rather than recomputed so that every caller gets the identical value.

The same package runs as a command line tool, an MCP server for agents, and in a browser through WebAssembly with nothing uploaded.

The method is not novel and this record says so. EGAD shipped node-degree AUROC as a built-in null in 2017 (doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btw695), Crow et al. PNAS 2019 did the cross-dataset version, and GREAT (doi:10.1038/nbt.1630) already corrects region-size bias. What is offered here is the null computed identically for everyone, versioned, hashed and callable.

The tool refuses to nominate candidates. It reports properties of rankings, never of the genes or gene sets in them; guide-pair concordance in the underlying screen is -0.019, so no gene-level claim is made anywhere and the build fails if one appears.

Boundary condition. Where hits are counted over the set's own members, a large R-squared is arithmetic before it is a confound, and the no-biology value is not zero. The tool states this at runtime and the documentation states it as scope limit 6.

Reference data: BioGRID ORCS 2.0.18 (Oughtred R et al., Protein Science 2021;30(1):187-200, doi:10.1002/pro.3978).
